questions.q: What does this lesson say Chapter 5's deliverables are actually for, once Chapter 6 begins?
options: They are defense preparation — material to reference and point to under questioning, not re-derive live
They are archival paperwork with no further use
They must be entirely rewritten before the defense can begin
They are only useful if the ARB specifically requests them in advance
questions.explain: The lesson reframes the diagrams, risk register, ADRs, and roadmap as the actual tools used during live questioning, not just documents produced and set aside.

questions.q: Which evaluation domain checks whether the data model from Lesson 9 'holds up after two years of real-world edge cases'?
options: Requirements traceability
Governance and maintainability
Data model and data quality
Risk and tradeoffs
questions.explain: The data model and data quality domain specifically evaluates whether the design will still make sense after real-world usage and edge cases, not just at initial build.

questions.q: What rehearsal method does this lesson recommend for the five ADRs from Lesson 25?
options: Memorizing the TAD word for word
Practicing stating the decision, the rejected alternative, and the reason for rejection out loud, in under thirty seconds, with no notes
Writing a new ADR for every possible board question in advance
Avoiding any mention of rejected alternatives during rehearsal
questions.explain: The lesson's specific rehearsal method is a timed, notes-free recitation of each ADR's decision, rejected alternative, and reason — fluency here is the actual goal.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say 'I don't know, but here's how I'd find out' can be a legitimate, strong answer during the defense?
options: Because it avoids the question entirely without consequence
Because ARBs penalize any answer that isn't a specific number
Because board members never ask about details not covered in this capstone's lessons
Because naming the correct mechanism to resolve a gap demonstrates knowing where the answer lives, which is stronger than inventing a confident-sounding guess
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly contrasts admitting a gap while naming the right mechanism to resolve it against inventing a confident but unfounded answer — the former is the stronger, more credible response.

questions.q: What does 'readiness' for Chapter 6 actually mean, per this lesson?
options: Being able to explain any of the thirteen design areas unprompted — what, why, and what was rejected — without needing to open the TAD
Memorizing every lesson's exact wording verbatim
Having a perfect, pre-written script for every possible question with no room for live reasoning
Completing Lessons 30 and 31 is sufficient on its own, without any further practice
questions.explain: Readiness is defined as unprompted fluency across what was decided, why, and what alternatives were rejected — not verbatim memorization, which Lessons 30 and 31 then test directly.
